sections.b: Chapters 1 to 4 hold the book's first two rounds. Round one (1:2-2:13) is a lawsuit against Samaria and then Judah: the LORD comes down, Samaria is ruined, Micah mourns the towns of the Shephelah, the land-grabbers are condemned, and the chapter ends with a promise of the remnant. Round two (3:1-5:15, the first part of it here) opens with a second "Hear" against the rulers and prophets, ends its judgment with Zion plowed like a field (3:12), and turns to the mountain of the LORD's house, the lame as a remnant, labor pains, Babylon and the threshing floor (4:1-13).

common: Micah is a prophet of the 700s BC from the Shephelah who spoke against Judah's rulers and promised a restored Zion.
uncommon: Some critics hold that most of chapters 4 and 5 and the end of chapter 7 come from after the exile; others defend them as Micah's.

sections.b: Micah 1:2-7 pronounces the ruin of Samaria: it will be a heap in the open country, its stones rolled into the valley, its carved images smashed and its wages burned. The sin is traced to the capital: "Who is behind Jacob's rebellion? Is it not Samaria?" (1:5). The fall came in 722/721 BC. The same verse turns the charge on Jerusalem.

sections.h: Jerusalem judged and exalted in Micah 1 to 4
sections.b: Micah names Jerusalem as the source of Judah's high places (1:5), says the wound that struck Samaria has reached its gate (1:9, 12), accuses its rulers of building it with blood (3:10) and announces that it will be heaps of rubble (3:12). The next chapter answers with the LORD's word going out from Jerusalem to the nations (4:2) and the kingdom coming to "Daughter Jerusalem" (4:8).

sections.h: The mountain of the LORD's house (Micah 3:12; 4:1-7)
sections.b: Micah sets two pictures of the same mountain side by side. In 3:12 it is a plowed field and a wooded height. In 4:1 it is set firm at the head of the mountains, lifted above the hills, and the peoples run to it for teaching. In 4:7 the LORD will be king over the remnant on Mount Zion from then on. The oracle of 4:1-3 is also in Isaiah 2:2-4.

common: Zion is the mountain of Jerusalem's Temple, where the LORD is said to dwell.

sections.b: Assyria is the unnamed power behind Micah 1: the siege and fall of Samaria (722/721 BC), the deportation of its people and the march through the Shephelah in 701 BC, when Sennacherib took Lachish and 46 other walled cities by his own count. Micah does not name Assyria in these chapters, but the exile in 1:16 and the ruin of Samaria are its work. The Plain notes the Assyrian reliefs at Nineveh that show the siege of Lachish.

The only mention of Babylon in the 8th-century prophet is in 4:10: "You will go as far as Babylon. There you will be rescued, and there the LORD will redeem you." Critical scholars often take it to come from the exile; others point to Isaiah 39:6-7, which tells Hezekiah in the same years that his house will be carried off to Babylon. The Greek and the scroll Mur88 both read "as far as Babylon".

common: Babylon here is the place of the exile after 586 BC.
uncommon: Micah foresaw the exile in Babylon in the 700s BC, as Isaiah did.

sections.b: Micah's remnant verses are hopeful. "I will gather you, all of you, Jacob... I will bring together what is left of Israel" (2:12). The lame and the driven-off are made "a remnant" and "a mighty nation" under the LORD's kingship on Zion (4:6-7). The remnant is not a few chosen strong ones but the weakest, whom the LORD himself gathers.

Micah 4:1-3 opens "In the days to come" (Hebrew be'acharit hayyamim) and describes the nations coming to Zion for the LORD's teaching, judging between peoples and ending war. The same oracle opens Isaiah 2:2-4. The phrase means "in the later part of the days": the future seen from the prophet's day, with a range from "later" to "the end". Christian writers from Justin on read the fulfillment in Christ and the church; others look for a future age.

Micah 1:3-4 describes the LORD leaving his place, coming down, treading the earth's high places while mountains melt and valleys split. It is the picture of the LORD's day of judgment as a storm of nature and war, used against Samaria first. Micah never uses the phrase "day of the LORD" in chapters 1 to 4, but "on that day" (2:4; 4:6) and "in the days to come" (4:1) mark the times of judgment and restoration.

Micah accuses Judah's rulers of the opposite of what the word mishpat means. They plan harm on their beds and take fields and houses (2:1-2). They "hate good and love evil" and flay the people like meat for the pot (3:2-3). They "abhor justice and bend crooked everything that is straight" (3:9), and their judges, priests and prophets each take payment (3:11). Micah asks, "Should you not be the ones who know justice?" (3:1) and claims for himself "justice and might" through the LORD's Spirit (3:8).

Micah 2 describes how the poor lose their homes: men crave fields and take them, crush a man and his household and the land he inherited (2:2), strip coats from passers-by (2:8) and throw women out of the houses they love (2:9). The law that the land is the LORD's and the family's share not to be sold for good (Leviticus 25:23; Numbers 36:7) is the background. The remedy promised in 4:4 is that each one sits under their own vine and fig tree.

The LORD gathers Jacob "like sheep in an enclosure, like a herd in the middle of its pasture" (2:12), and the breaker goes up in front of them, with their king and the LORD at their head (2:13). In 4:8 the "Tower of the Flock" (Migdal-eder), near Bethlehem on Genesis 35:21, is addressed as the place where the first dominion will return. The shepherd-king image is developed in the other part of this book.

Micah's opponents say "Do not rant" (2:6), and the people would prefer a prophet full of wind who promised wine and beer (2:11). The prophets who lead the people astray shout "Peace!" for those who feed them and declare holy war on those who do not (3:5). They will have night in place of visions (3:6). Micah answers by claiming the LORD's Spirit, justice and might to tell Jacob his rebellion (3:8).

common: A true prophet's message does not depend on his payment.

sections.b: Micah is dated to the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:1). Jeremiah 26:18-19 says the sentence of 3:12 was spoken in Hezekiah's days, and that Hezekiah did not kill Micah but feared the LORD, and the LORD changed his mind about the harm. Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BC, the likely setting of 1:10-16, ended with Jerusalem spared (2 Kings 19:35-36).

Bamot, "high places", names the earth's heights under the LORD's feet (1:3) and the hilltop shrines of Judah, which Micah says are in Jerusalem (1:5). The Temple mountain itself will be reduced to "high ground in a forest" (3:12). The word is the same in all three places.

Micah 1:7 lists carved images to be beaten to pieces, wages to burn, and idols to be made a wasteland. The wealth of Samaria's worship is called "a prostitute's pay", as in Hosea 9:1. The two scrolls that preserve the verse, 4Q82 and Mur88, agree with the Masoretic Text.

The title first appears in 1:13, where Lachish was "the start of sin for Daughter Zion". It returns in 4:8 (the kingdom of Daughter Jerusalem), in 4:10 ("Twist in pain and push, Daughter Zion") and in 4:13 ("Get up and thresh, Daughter Zion"). The city is addressed as a woman in labor, a threshing ox and a daughter whose kingdom returns.

Micah 4:8 promises that to the Tower of the Flock, the hill of Daughter Zion, "the first dominion will come, the kingdom of Daughter Jerusalem": the kingdom of David and Solomon restored. It prepares for the ruler from Bethlehem in 5:2, in the other part of this book. The Targum of the Minor Prophets is reported to read the "Tower of the Flock" as the Messiah of Israel (not checked against the Aramaic).

In the Hebrew order Micah is the sixth of the Twelve, between Jonah and Nahum; in the Greek order he is the third, between Amos and Joel. Micah's call, "Hear this, peoples, every one of you" (1:2), echoes the prophet Micaiah (1 Kings 22:28). The vision of the nations at Zion (4:1-3) is also in Isaiah 2, and Joel 3:10 reverses its line about plowshares.

In Micah the saying comes with the Hebrew words that Isaiah lacks: the LORD judges "between many peoples" and sets things right for "mighty nations, however far away" (4:3), and the next verse adds that each person will sit under their own vine and fig tree and no one will terrify them (4:4). Micah then closes the oracle with the people's answer (4:5): all peoples walk each in the name of its god, "but we will walk in the name of the LORD our God for ever and ever." Justin, Irenaeus and Origen read the saying as fulfilled in Christ or as a call to Christians not to fight. A sculpture in the garden of the United Nations in New York, "Let Us Beat Swords into Plowshares" (Evgeniy Vuchetich, a gift of the Soviet Union in 1959), takes its title from it.

sections.h: The Temple mountain in Micah 3 and 4
sections.b: Micah 3:12 says the mountain of the house (the Temple Mount) will be high ground in a forest; Micah 4:1 says the mountain where the LORD's house stands will be set firm at the head of the mountains. The rulers who said "Is the LORD not in the middle of us?" (3:11) trusted the Temple; Jeremiah 7:4 meets the same trust with the same answer.

The word "exile" first occurs in 1:16, where children go into exile away from the mother shaving her head. In 2:10 the LORD tells his people, "Get up and go!" because the land is unclean. In 4:6-7 the LORD gathers the lame and the driven-off, and in 4:10 Daughter Zion leaves the city for the open country and goes as far as Babylon, where the LORD will rescue and redeem her.

Micah 3:8 is one of the few places in the pre-exilic writing prophets where the prophet says the Spirit of the LORD is with him: "I am full of strength: the LORD's Spirit is with me, along with justice and might, so I can tell Jacob his rebellion." It is set against the false prophet who walks in "wind" (the same Hebrew word, ruach) and lies (2:11), and against the question of 2:7, "Is the LORD's Spirit cut short?"

Micah's book opens as a word he "saw" (1:1) and claims the Spirit's power for his preaching (3:8). Jeremiah's elders quote 3:12 by name and date about a hundred years later (Jeremiah 26:17-19), the plainest case of one prophet's words quoted as authority by another's hearers. Micah's opponents try to silence him with the order "Do not rant" (2:6), as Amaziah tells Amos (Amos 7:16).

sections.h: Women put out of their homes (Micah 2:9)
sections.b: Micah 2:9 charges the powerful with throwing "the women of my people... out of the houses they love" and taking "my honor" from their children. These are probably widows and their children, who lost house and land when a head of household died or fell into debt. It belongs with the laws and prophetic charges for widows and orphans.

sections.h: The nations on the threshing floor (Micah 4:12-13)
sections.b: Micah 4:12 says the nations that gathered against Zion do not know that the LORD has gathered them like cut grain onto the threshing floor. In 4:13 Zion is told, "Get up and thresh," with horn of iron and hooves of bronze, as an ox beating out grain, and to set apart the nations' stolen gain for the LORD.

At Jeremiah's trial the elders quote Micah 3:12: "Zion will be plowed like a field. Jerusalem will be heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the house will be high ground in a forest." The Hebrew of the two verses is the same word for word, and Jeremiah's Hebrew text writes Micah's name in the longer spelling Mikhayah.

Micah 3:5 says the false prophets "declare a holy war" (literally "consecrate war") against whoever puts nothing in their mouths. In 4:13 the LORD tells Daughter Zion that he will "set apart for destruction" the nations' stolen gain for himself, the language of the ban (Joshua 6:17-19).

The prophet's own mourning in Micah 1:8 ("I will mourn and howl. I will walk around barefoot and stripped bare") opens a lament built on the names of towns, ending with the call to a mother to shave her head for children taken into exile (1:16). The poem uses the cries of jackals and ostriches for the sound of grief.

Micah 2:2 and 2:5 treat the land as an inheritance shared out by lot in the LORD's assembly. The men who seize it have no share the next time the lot is cast (2:5). "This is no resting place" (2:10) reverses the promised "resting place" of Deuteronomy 12:9.
Micah 1:13 addresses the people of Lachish: "hitch the swift horses to the chariot." Lachish was the chief fortress of the Shephelah and Sennacherib's headquarters in 701 BC.

Micah 1:3-4 uses the pattern of the Divine Warrior: the LORD leaves his place, comes down, treads the heights of the earth, and the mountains melt like wax and the valleys split. Here the warrior comes as a witness against his own people (1:2), and the first target is Samaria.

Micah 1:2 opens the first of three "Hear" speeches by summoning all the peoples and the earth as witnesses: "Let the Lord GOD stand as a witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple." The setting is a court; the charge is Jacob's rebellion (1:5). The third "Hear" speech, the full lawsuit, is in 6:1-8.

Micah 3:2-3 describes the rulers' treatment of the people in the language of butchery: ripping off skin, breaking bones, chopping them up like meat for the pot. The picture is of violence done through judgments, taxes and seizure, not necessarily by hand. Psalm 14:4 and Ezekiel 11:3 use related images.
